commands.name: ls
commands.summary: List directory contents with optional detail and sorting.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only operation, no system changes.
commands.explanation: ls reads directory entries and displays them. With -l it shows permissions, ownership, size, and timestamps. -a reveals hidden dotfiles. Pipe to grep or awk for filtering. Colors are controlled by LS_COLORS.

flags.desc: Long format: permissions, links, owner, size, date
Print sizes as K, M, G instead of bytes
Sort by modification time, newest first
Sort by file size, largest first

examples.desc: Show all files including hidden with human-readable sizes in /var/log
Show the 20 most recently modified files in /tmp

commands.pro_tip: Use `ls --color=always | less -R` to get colorized output inside less without losing terminal color codes.

commands.name: cd
commands.summary: Change the current working directory.
commands.risk_reason: Navigation only, no file modifications.
commands.explanation: cd updates the shell's working directory. `cd -` returns to the previous directory. `cd ~` always goes home. In scripts, always pair cd with `|| exit 1` to catch failure before running destructive follow-up commands.

examples.desc: Jump back to the previous directory
Go to your home directory from anywhere

commands.pro_tip: Use `pushd /path` and `popd` when you need a directory stack — navigate away and return without remembering the original path.

commands.name: pwd
commands.summary: Print the full absolute path of the current working directory.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only, purely informational.
commands.explanation: pwd resolves and prints the absolute path. -P shows the physical path resolving symlinks, useful after cd-ing through symlinked directories. The $PWD variable is always available as an alternative.

flags.desc: Print real physical path, resolving all symlinks
Use shell logical path including symlinks (default)

examples.desc: Show real path resolving any symlinks
Capture current directory into a variable in a script

commands.pro_tip: In bash scripts use `$PWD` built-in variable instead of calling `$(pwd)` — it's faster since it avoids spawning a subshell.

commands.name: cp
commands.summary: Copy files or directories from source to destination.
commands.risk_reason: Can silently overwrite destination files without warning.
cautions: Silently overwrites existing files — use -i (ask) or -n (never).
With -r, a trailing slash or an existing destination changes where things end up; check with ls afterwards.
Permissions, ownership and timestamps are only preserved with -a / -p.
commands.explanation: cp copies files and directories. Without -r it refuses to copy directories. -p preserves timestamps and permissions — critical for backups. -u only copies when source is newer. The -i flag adds interactive prompts before overwriting.

flags.desc: Copy directories and all their contents recursively
Copy only when source is newer than destination
Print each file as it is copied

examples.desc: Backup nginx config recursively with preserved permissions
Copy config with confirmation prompt if destination exists
Archive-copy all files verbosely showing each transfer

commands.pro_tip: Prefer `rsync -a` over `cp -r` for large directories — rsync is resumable, shows progress, and handles edge cases better.

commands.name: mv
commands.summary: Move or rename files and directories.
commands.risk_reason: Overwrites destination without warning and cannot be undone.
cautions: Overwrites the destination without asking (unless -i/-n).
Across filesystems mv is copy + delete — an interruption leaves partial data.
If the target directory does not exist, mv renames the source instead of moving it into a directory.
commands.explanation: mv moves or renames files. Cross-filesystem moves copy then delete. Use -i for safety in scripts. Unlike cp, the original is always removed after a successful move.

flags.desc: Create a backup of each overwritten file

examples.desc: Rename file as backup before editing
Move all deploy files to web root verbosely
Move all log files to archive with overwrite confirmation

commands.pro_tip: Use `mv -b` to auto-create tilde-suffixed backups (~) on overwrite — great for safe config file rotation.

commands.name: rm
commands.summary: Remove files or directories permanently with no recycle bin.
commands.risk_reason: Permanently deletes files. No undo. No trash. Irreversible.
cautions: No trash, no undo — deleted files are gone.
Preview with `ls` or `echo rm …` first, especially with globs and variables.
Never run `rm -rf` with a variable that might be empty or unquoted.
rm does not ask before deleting files you can write; use -i or -I to be prompted.
commands.explanation: rm deletes files immediately. There is no recycle bin on Linux. The -rf combination recursively forces deletion — extremely dangerous near / or $HOME. Always double-check paths in scripts and never use unquoted variables.

flags.desc: Remove directories and all their contents
Show each file as it is removed

examples.desc: Safer: find and delete tmp files without rm -rf

safer.why: Preview what you are about to delete.
Ask once before a recursive delete (-I); use -i to be asked for every file.
Move to the trash (trash-cli) so it can be recovered.

commands.pro_tip: Never run `rm -rf $VAR/path` — if $VAR is empty it becomes `rm -rf /path`. Always validate and quote variables before destructive commands.

commands.name: mkdir
commands.summary: Create one or more new directories.
commands.risk_reason: Creates directories only, no destructive action.
commands.explanation: mkdir creates directories. The -p flag creates all parent directories as needed and suppresses errors if already existing — ideal for idempotent scripts and CI pipelines.

flags.desc: Create parent dirs as needed, no error if existing
Set permissions for the new directory (like chmod)
Print a message for each created directory

examples.desc: Create app directory with three subdirectories via brace expansion
Create .ssh directory with strict owner-only permissions

commands.pro_tip: Use brace expansion `mkdir -p project/{src,tests,docs,bin}` to scaffold entire project structures in one command.

commands.name: find
commands.summary: Recursively search for files by name, type, size, time, and more.
commands.risk_reason: Combined with -exec rm, can delete files at scale.
cautions: Always run with -print first; only add -delete or -exec rm once the list is right.
-delete must be the LAST expression — tests placed after it do not limit what is deleted.
Searching / is slow and loads production disks; scope the path and add -xdev.
commands.explanation: find is the most powerful file search tool on Linux. It supports filtering by name, type, permissions, size, modification time, and more — and can execute arbitrary commands on matches with -exec. Essential for cleanup, auditing, and automation.

flags.desc: Filter by type: f (file), d (dir), l (symlink)
Match by modification time in days

examples.desc: Delete log files older than 30 days
Find large files in home directories
Files newer than a reference file

commands.pro_tip: Use `-exec cmd {} +` instead of `-exec cmd {} \;` — the `+` variant batches arguments (like xargs), dramatically faster for large result sets.

commands.name: tar
commands.summary: Archive and compress files — the standard Linux backup and packaging tool.
commands.risk_reason: Extraction can overwrite existing files; archives may contain absolute paths.
cautions: Extraction overwrites existing files silently — list first with `tar -tf`.
Archives can contain absolute paths or ../ entries; inspect before extracting as root.
Use -C <dir> to control where files are extracted.
commands.explanation: tar bundles files into an archive. Combined with gzip (-z), bzip2 (-j), or xz (-J) it compresses too. The -C flag changes extraction directory. Always inspect archives with -t before extracting to avoid surprises.

flags.desc: Compress/decompress with xz (.tar.xz) — best compression ratio

examples.desc: Create date-stamped compressed backup of web root
Preview compressed archive contents before extracting

commands.pro_tip: Exclude directories on archive: `tar --exclude='./logs' --exclude='./.git' -czf archive.tar.gz .`

commands.name: rsync
commands.summary: Fast, resumable file synchronization tool — local or over SSH.
commands.risk_reason: --delete removes destination files not in source — use with caution.
cautions: A trailing slash matters: `src/` copies the contents, `src` copies the directory itself.
--delete removes destination files that are not in the source — always run with -n (dry run) first.
Use -a to preserve attributes; -c (checksums) is expensive on big trees.
commands.explanation: rsync transfers only changed file blocks (delta transfer) making it extremely efficient. -a preserves permissions, timestamps, symlinks, and ownership. --delete mirrors the source exactly. Always test with -n (dry-run) first.

flags.desc: Archive: recursive + preserve perms, times, symlinks, owner
Delete destination files not in source (mirror mode)

examples.desc: Sync web root to remote server with progress display
Dry-run to preview what would sync before committing

commands.pro_tip: Always test with `rsync -avn` (dry run) before using `--delete`. One typo in the source path could wipe your entire destination.

commands.name: df
commands.summary: Report disk space usage of mounted filesystems.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only filesystem inspection.
commands.explanation: df shows disk space for each filesystem. -h makes sizes human-readable. -T shows the filesystem type (ext4, xfs, tmpfs). Filter with grep to exclude tmpfs mounts in containers which can clutter output.

flags.desc: Show sizes in K, M, G, T
Show inode usage instead of block usage

examples.desc: Show real disk usage excluding temporary filesystems
Check inode usage on root — exhaustion prevents new files even with free space
All filesystem usage with a total summary line

commands.pro_tip: A disk can show free space but give 'No space left on device' — always check inodes with `df -i` too.

commands.name: du
commands.summary: Estimate disk usage of files and directories.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only — scans disk usage without modifications.
cautions: Scanning huge trees (e.g. / or network mounts) causes heavy I/O — scope the path and use -x to stay on one filesystem.
commands.explanation: du walks the directory tree summing file sizes. -s gives a total for each argument. --max-depth limits recursion depth. Piping to `sort -rh` reveals the biggest disk consumers — essential for tracking down space hogs.

flags.desc: Display only a total for each argument
Include all files, not just directories

examples.desc: Show size of each item in /var/log
Find top 20 largest directories from root
Get total size of current directory excluding .git

commands.pro_tip: Install `ncdu` for an interactive disk usage explorer: `sudo apt install ncdu && ncdu /`

commands.name: scp
commands.summary: Securely copy files between local and remote hosts over SSH.
commands.risk_reason: Can overwrite remote files silently; key misuse is a risk.
cautions: Overwrites remote files silently; the legacy SCP protocol is deprecated — prefer rsync or sftp.
Wildcards are also expanded on the remote side; quote them.
Verify the host key fingerprint on first connection.
commands.explanation: scp uses SSH to transfer files. -r copies directories. Note: -P (capital) sets the port for scp, unlike ssh which uses lowercase -p. For large or resumable transfers prefer rsync.

examples.desc: Download nginx config directory preserving timestamps
Upload large file over non-standard port with compression

commands.pro_tip: For anything over a few MB, use `rsync -avz --progress` instead — it resumes interrupted transfers automatically.

commands.name: gzip
commands.summary: Compress or decompress files using the GNU zip DEFLATE algorithm.
commands.risk_reason: Replaces the original file by default — original is deleted after compression.
commands.explanation: gzip compresses a single file and replaces it with a .gz version. -k keeps the original. -d decompresses (same as gunzip). Compression level -1 (fastest) through -9 (best ratio). Combine with tar for multi-file archives.

flags.desc: Decompress a .gz file (same as running gunzip)
Keep the original file after compressing
Write output to stdout, don't replace file
Recursively compress all files in a directory
Show compression ratio and sizes for .gz files
Show compression ratio for each file processed

examples.desc: Compress SQL dump with best ratio, keeping the original file
Decompress a .gz file back to its original form
Show compression stats (ratio, original vs compressed size) for all .gz files

commands.pro_tip: Use `zcat file.gz | grep pattern` to search inside a compressed file without decompressing it to disk first.

commands.name: stat
commands.summary: Display detailed metadata about files and filesystems.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: stat shows comprehensive file metadata: inode number, permissions in both octal and symbolic form, link count, ownership, file size, and all three timestamps (access, modify, change). Far more informative than ls -l for debugging permission and timing issues.

examples.desc: Show full metadata including timestamps and permissions
Print octal permissions and filename only

commands.pro_tip: Use `stat -c '%a'` in scripts to check exact octal permissions — more reliable than parsing `ls -l` output which varies by implementation.

commands.name: ln
commands.summary: Create hard or symbolic links between files.
commands.risk_reason: Dangling symlinks and circular links can cause confusion.
cautions: `ln -sf` replaces an existing link/file at the target without asking.
Relative symlinks are resolved from the link’s directory, not your current directory.
Hard links cannot cross filesystems or point to directories.
commands.explanation: ln creates links — hard links share the same inode (same data, different name), while symbolic links (-s) are pointers to a path. Symlinks are the standard choice: they work across filesystems, can link directories, and make the relationship explicit.

flags.desc: Treat symlink destination as normal file

commands.pro_tip: Use symlinks for version-managed deployments: keep versioned dirs (/opt/app/v1.2.3) and update a single symlink (/opt/app/current) for instant, reversible deploys.

commands.name: readlink
commands.summary: Resolve and display the target of a symbolic link.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: readlink prints the target of a symlink. The -f flag canonicalizes the entire path, resolving all nested symlinks and relative components — essential for finding the true absolute path of any file.

flags.desc: Resolve all symlinks to absolute path
Canonicalize, fail if path doesn't exist
Canonicalize even if path doesn't exist

examples.desc: Get absolute path of current script

commands.pro_tip: Use `readlink -f $0` at the top of shell scripts to get the script's actual directory regardless of how it was invoked — essential for portable scripts.

commands.name: file
commands.summary: Determine file type by inspecting content (not extension).
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: file tests files and reports their type based on magic bytes in the content, not the filename extension. Crucial for identifying mislabeled files, checking if a binary is ELF/ARM/x86, verifying compressed archives, and examining unknown files safely.

examples.desc: Show ELF architecture of a binary
Verify actual file type regardless of extension

commands.pro_tip: Use `file` before executing or extracting unknown files — it reveals if a '.jpg' is actually a shell script or if a binary was compiled for the wrong architecture.

commands.name: xz
commands.summary: High-ratio compression using the XZ/LZMA algorithm.
commands.risk_reason: Deletes source file by default; use -k to keep it.
commands.explanation: xz provides high compression ratios using the LZMA2 algorithm — better compression than gzip at the cost of more CPU and memory. Widely used for distributing Linux kernel tarballs and large datasets. Works like gzip in its pipeline behavior.
commands.pro_tip: Use `xz -T 0` to enable multi-threaded compression on large files — xz is single-threaded by default and can be extremely slow without this flag.

commands.name: zstd
commands.summary: Fast, modern compression with excellent speed/ratio trade-off.
commands.risk_reason: Deletes source by default; use -k to keep.
commands.explanation: zstd (Zstandard) offers near-gzip speed with compression ratios approaching xz. The --fast flag prioritizes speed; higher -N levels improve ratio. Now the default compression for Linux kernel packages and increasingly common in DevOps tooling.
commands.pro_tip: For backup pipelines, zstd is the modern choice: `tar c /data | zstd -T 0 -9 -o backup.tar.zst` — 3-4x faster than xz with only slightly worse compression.

commands.name: tree
commands.summary: Show a directory tree
commands.risk_reason: Read-only listing; large trees can be slow and noisy.
commands.explanation: Prints directories and files as an indented tree. Useful for understanding project layouts.
commands.pro_tip: Use -L on large trees — an unbounded tree of / floods the terminal.

commands.name: touch
commands.summary: Create an empty file or update timestamps
commands.risk_reason: Only creates files or changes timestamps.
cautions: Changing mtimes can confuse backups, rsync and build systems that rely on timestamps.
commands.explanation: Creates the file if it does not exist, otherwise updates its modification time. Often used to create placeholders or reset mtime for make/rsync.

examples.desc: Give b.txt the same mtime as a.txt

commands.name: rmdir
commands.summary: Remove empty directories
commands.risk_reason: Refuses to delete non-empty directories, so it is safe by design.
commands.explanation: Deletes directories only if they are empty — a safer alternative to rm -r when you expect nothing to be inside.

flags.desc: Remove parent directories too if they become empty
Do not complain about non-empty directories

examples.desc: Remove c, then b and a if empty

commands.pro_tip: Prefer rmdir over rm -r when the directory should be empty — it fails loudly if it is not.

commands.name: cat
commands.summary: Print or concatenate files
commands.risk_reason: Read-only, but can dump secrets or binary data to the terminal.
cautions: `cat > file` and `cat file > file` overwrite or truncate files — `cat a b > a` destroys a.
Avoid cat on binary files; it can corrupt your terminal (use `reset` to recover). Use less or strings instead.
Do not cat files containing secrets in shared terminals or recorded sessions.
commands.explanation: Concatenates files to standard output. Also used to create small files with redirection.

flags.desc: Show non-printing characters, tabs and line ends

commands.pro_tip: Useless use of cat: prefer `grep pattern file` over `cat file | grep pattern`.

commands.name: basename
commands.summary: Strip directory from a path
commands.risk_reason: Pure string manipulation.
commands.explanation: Prints the final component of a path and optionally strips a suffix.

commands.name: dirname
commands.summary: Strip last component from a path
commands.risk_reason: Pure string manipulation.
commands.explanation: Prints the directory portion of a path (everything before the last slash); handy in scripts to locate sibling files.

commands.name: realpath
commands.summary: Resolve a path to its absolute form
commands.risk_reason: Read-only path resolution.
commands.explanation: Prints the absolute canonical path, resolving symlinks and .. components.

flags.desc: Print path relative to a directory

commands.name: locate
commands.summary: Find files by name using an index
commands.risk_reason: Reads a prebuilt database; results may be stale or reveal paths you did not expect to see.
cautions: The index may list files that were deleted, or hide new ones, until updatedb runs.
commands.explanation: Searches an index of filenames built by updatedb — much faster than find but only as fresh as the last index run.

examples.desc: Count log files in the index

commands.name: updatedb
commands.summary: Rebuild the locate database
commands.risk_reason: Scans the entire filesystem and causes noticeable disk I/O.
cautions: Heavy I/O on large or network filesystems — avoid during peak hours on production hosts.
The database may expose the names of files other users cannot read on some systems; check mlocate/plocate permissions.
commands.explanation: Walks the filesystem and rewrites the database used by locate. Normally run from cron daily.

commands.name: split
commands.summary: Split a file into pieces
commands.risk_reason: Creates many new files in the current directory.
cautions: Output files go to the current directory — run it in an empty one.
Reassemble with `cat part_* > file` and verify with a checksum.
commands.explanation: Splits a file by size or line count into numbered chunks.

flags.desc: Append a suffix to chunk names

commands.name: cmp
commands.summary: Compare two files byte by byte
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Reports the first byte where two files differ — fast for binary files.

commands.name: sha256sum
commands.summary: Compute or verify SHA-256 checksums
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
cautions: A checksum only proves integrity relative to the checksum you compare against — fetch it from a trusted channel over HTTPS (or verify a GPG signature).
Do not use md5sum/sha1sum for security decisions.
commands.explanation: Prints or verifies SHA-256 digests; use to confirm downloads and backups are intact.

flags.desc: Skip files that are not present

examples.desc: Verify files listed in a checksum file

commands.name: md5sum
commands.summary: Compute or verify MD5 checksums
commands.risk_reason: Read-only, but MD5 is cryptographically broken.
cautions: MD5 collisions can be forged — never rely on it to authenticate downloads; use sha256sum.
commands.explanation: Prints MD5 digests. Fine for accidental corruption checks, not for security.

commands.name: truncate
commands.summary: Shrink or extend a file to a size
commands.risk_reason: Cutting a file shorter permanently discards data beyond the new size.
cautions: Data past the new size is gone — there is no undo.
Truncating a log that a process holds open is usually fine, but truncating a database or data file corrupts it.
Check the filename carefully; this runs without confirmation.
commands.explanation: Sets a file to an exact size. `truncate -s 0 file` empties it without deleting it; extending creates a sparse file.

examples.desc: Empty a log file in place (keeps inode)

commands.name: install
commands.summary: Copy files and set mode/owner
commands.risk_reason: Overwrites the destination and sets permissions/ownership in one step.
cautions: Overwrites an existing destination without asking.
Wrong -m/-o on files under /usr or /etc can open security holes or break services.
commands.explanation: Copies files like cp but sets mode (-m), owner (-o) and group (-g) and can create parent directories (-D).

commands.name: lsattr
commands.summary: List file attributes
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Shows extended attributes such as immutable (i) and append-only (a) flags on ext filesystems.

commands.name: chattr
commands.summary: Change file attributes (immutable, append-only)
commands.risk_reason: Immutable files cannot be changed or deleted even by root until the flag is removed; mistakes cause confusing failures.
cautions: An immutable /etc file makes package upgrades and config management fail with “Operation not permitted”.
Applying +i recursively to system directories can prevent boot, updates and logging.
Document every immutable file — future admins will not expect it.
commands.explanation: Sets ext2/3/4 attributes. +i makes a file immutable, +a append-only.

safer.why: Undo immutability if things stop working

commands.name: getfacl
commands.summary: Show file access control lists
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Displays ACL entries beyond the basic owner/group/other permissions.

examples.desc: Back up ACLs before changing them

commands.name: setfacl
commands.summary: Set file access control lists
commands.risk_reason: Changes who can read/write files; recursive mistakes expose data or lock users out.
cautions: Back up first: getfacl -R path > acl.bak (restore with setfacl --restore=acl.bak).
-b -R removes every ACL under the tree.
ACLs are easy to forget — review with getfacl during audits.
commands.explanation: Adds, modifies or removes ACL entries. Use for fine-grained sharing without changing groups.

flags.desc: Set default ACL for new files

examples.desc: Recursive read access for a group

commands.name: zip
commands.summary: Create ZIP archives
commands.risk_reason: Creates a new file; can overwrite an existing archive name.
cautions: `zip -e` uses weak encryption and the password is easy to leak via shell history — use gpg or age for sensitive data.
Existing archives are updated, not replaced — delete the old zip first if you want a clean archive.
commands.explanation: Packs files into a .zip archive (portable to Windows/macOS).

flags.desc: Encrypt with a password (weak legacy encryption)

commands.name: unzip
commands.summary: Extract ZIP archives
commands.risk_reason: Silently overwrites existing files and may write outside the target (zip-slip) with malicious archives.
cautions: -o overwrites existing files with no prompt.
Inspect untrusted archives with `unzip -l` first; extract into an empty directory.
commands.explanation: Extracts .zip files; -l lists contents without extracting.

commands.name: gunzip
commands.summary: Decompress gzip files
commands.risk_reason: Replaces the .gz file with the decompressed file by default.
cautions: Without -k the original .gz is deleted — keep it if the source copy is your only backup.
commands.explanation: Equivalent to gzip -d; removes the .gz after decompressing unless -k is used.

commands.name: zcat
commands.summary: Print compressed file contents
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Decompresses gzip files to stdout without touching the file — great for rotated logs.

commands.name: zgrep
commands.summary: Search inside gzip files
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: grep for compressed files; ideal for rotated logs.

commands.name: bzip2
commands.summary: Compress files with bzip2
commands.risk_reason: Replaces the original file with the .bz2 version unless -k is used.
cautions: Without -k the original is deleted.
commands.explanation: Better compression than gzip at lower speed.

commands.name: ncdu
commands.summary: Interactive disk usage browser
commands.risk_reason: Scans disk (I/O heavy) but only deletes if you press d and confirm.
cautions: Pressing d deletes files — confirm carefully, especially as root.
Scanning large filesystems at peak time can slow production disks; use -x and run off-hours.
commands.explanation: A curses disk-usage analyzer. Navigate with arrows, press d to delete the selected item.

commands.name: pushd
commands.summary: Push a directory onto the stack and cd
commands.risk_reason: Only changes the shell’s working directory.
commands.explanation: Remember the current directory and switch to another; popd returns.

examples.desc: Go to /var/log and remember where you were

commands.name: popd
commands.summary: Return to the previous directory on the stack
commands.risk_reason: Shell builtin; only changes directory.
commands.explanation: Pops the directory stack and cds to the new top.

commands.name: dirs
commands.summary: Show the directory stack
commands.risk_reason: Shell builtin; read-only.
commands.explanation: Prints the directory stack maintained by pushd and popd; -v numbers the entries so you can jump with cd ~N.

commands.name: rename
commands.summary: Rename multiple files with a pattern
commands.risk_reason: Batch renames can overwrite or scramble many files at once.
cautions: Always run with -n first (Perl rename).
Two source files mapping to the same name overwrite each other with -f.
The Perl and util-linux versions have different syntax — check `rename --version`.
commands.explanation: Renames files using a Perl regex (Debian/Ubuntu) or a simple string substitution (util-linux). Syntax differs between implementations.

flags.desc: Dry run: show what would be renamed (Perl rename)

commands.name: shred
commands.summary: Overwrite a file to make recovery harder
commands.risk_reason: Destroys data irrecoverably; ineffective on journaling, SSD and copy-on-write filesystems.
cautions: Irreversible — there is no undo and no trash.
Does NOT reliably wipe data on SSDs, RAID, snapshots, btrfs/ZFS or journaled data — use full-disk encryption and secure erase.
Double-check the filename; a wrong target is lost for good.
commands.explanation: Overwrites a file multiple times, optionally deleting it (-u).

flags.desc: Add a final pass of zeros

commands.name: mkfifo
commands.summary: Create a named pipe
commands.risk_reason: Creates a special file; blocks readers/writers until both ends are open.
commands.explanation: Makes a FIFO that processes can use for inter-process communication.

examples.desc: Read from it (blocks until a writer appears)
